The voice is the oldest, most complex and most expressive instrument, and the hardest to imitate. Attempts to produce it outside the body go back to the 18th century, when Wolfgang von Kempelen built the first machine to produce intelligible speech. The 19th-century Euphonia was played with a keyboard and pedals like a small organ, and the Voder, the first electrical speech synthesizer, demanded virtuoso control of hand-operated filters and a pitch pedal.

Ulla Rauter’s own work began with spectrograms, the “fingerprints” of sound. After turning image scans into sine tones, she started drawing spectrograms by hand. In “Sound on Drawing” (Ton auf Zeichnung) she painted spectrograms of speech on walls in UV paint and sonified them with an inverse FFT; in “Sound Calligraphy” she draws symbols live, filmed and looped, so speech becomes intelligible as the strokes accumulate.

Her first live voice instrument, the Fingertip Vocoder, uses brass sensor rings on each finger to trigger a Pure Data patch that copies her voice at set intervals, so finger combinations produce chords and a one-woman choir. A Leap Motion controller later let her gestures place, move and freeze voices in 3D audio. In “Talking Hands,” hand tracking and an LED grid drive the DECtalk synthesizer and, later, an AI voice trained with Resemble AI. In the performance “All of My Voices,” the Voicebow maps her voice onto a single string to be plucked, struck or bowed. Next, she hopes to combine AI voice synthesis with real-time sensing of lips and tongue to build a playable virtual vocal tract.

Adapted into Chinese by Fanyu Meng from “The Human Voice as a Sensor-Based Electronic Live Instrument” by Ulla Rauter, published on Sounding Future. Read the original.
